3.1 — The Turret: Distance & the Detection Radius

Coins wait to be collected; spikes wait to be bumped into. The turret is the first thing in this game that decides. Build TurretController.cs from scratch — and notice which half of the job the physics engine does for you.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to get the distance between two objects, how to find an object by tag, how to detect when the player is within a radius”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

The turret notices me. That is the whole feature, and "how does a turret notice me" has no answer a computer can act on.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the turret a circle it can notice things insidewhat does this part do?Read: the Circle Collider 2D and Is Trigger steps from 2.1, and the Turret prefab's own Detection Radius child.
  2. Hold the answer as one true/false fieldwhat does this part do?Read: the class-body field rule from 1.3, and the bool you built for IsWalking in 1.6.
  3. Hear the player arrive, and hear them leavewhat does this part do?Read: the OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) callback from 2.1, and its exit twin.
  4. Remember who walked inwhat does this part do?Read: other.transform in the Unity scripting reference, and the Transform you have read since 1.2.

"Notice the player" is not something you can write. Each of these four is — and only one is about turrets. A trigger, a bool, two callbacks and a reference are ordinary tools you will reach for all year; the turret is just where they happen to combine.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the turret shoot" cannot be. "Do something when an object enters a trigger" can.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The table below prices two ways to answer "is the player close enough?" — a collider that tells you, and a distance you measure yourself. Say which this project uses and what that choice costs you.

In the Editor ~15 min
  1. Hierarchy → the Overworld scene, which holds two Turret instances. Then Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Turret → Inspector → an empty Turret Controller component is already attached: the script exists, it is wired up, and it does nothing — the same situation as PlayerController in Unit 1.
  2. Hierarchy → Turret → Detection Radius. Read the Circle Collider 2D: Radius 2, Is Trigger ticked. That circle is the turret's range. Drag the radius in the Scene view while Play is stopped and watch the green ring grow — that ring is the whole danger zone.
  3. Inspector → Detection Radius → Radius: give the two turrets in the Overworld different values and stand between them. One notices you before the other. Nothing in the script changed.
  4. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Player → Inspector → Rigidbody 2D: confirm it is there, Dynamic, Gravity Scale 0. The body you added in 2.1 is what makes a trigger fire at all — a trigger between two objects with no body is a circle that never notices anything.
  5. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Player, Inspector → Tag: confirm the exact spelling your script will ask for, on the object carrying the collider. A tag that does not match is not an error, it is silence.
  6. Once the code half is done — Game view → press Play and walk slowly toward a turret: quiet outside the ring, a line in the Console the moment you cross it, quiet again as you walk back out.
In the Code ~30 min

There are two ways to answer "is the player close enough?", and they are not the same amount of work. This project takes the first row.

ApproachWho does the measuringWhat you getWhat it costs
A trigger collider on a child, plus OnTriggerEnter2D() / OnTriggerExit2D() The physics engine. It tests shapes against shapes every step and sends you a message when the answer changes. An event on the way in and another on the way out, and a radius a designer drags in the Scene view. Nothing fires when an object appears inside the circle without crossing its edge; and the circle needs a body on one of the two objects to work at all.
Vector3.Distance(a, b) in Update(), compared against a range field You do, sixty times a second, whether anything changed or not. A real distance in world units — printable, and useful if you need how far. A square root every frame, a target reference you have to find yourself, and no event: you re-derive the same true or false forever.
[SerializeField] float range You, by typing a number. A tunable radius per instance. It is invisible: you cannot see it in the Scene view, so "the player was inside" and "the player was not" look identical until you print something.
other.gameObject.CompareTag("Player") The engine, on a tag comparison. Only the player counts — a coin rolling through the ring does not trip the turret. A tag is a promise nothing enforces: anything tagged Player will trip every turret in the scene.
Architectural specification for TurretController.cs:
  • Which object owns the circle, and why is it a child rather than the turret's own collider? What would happen if the turret's solid body were also the trigger?
  • What single field remembers that the player is inside, what type is it, and what value must it start at?
  • Which two callbacks does the radius produce, and what does each one set? Name the field each callback writes, and say what would break if only one existed.
  • What is stored in target, and why store it at all when Update() could look the player up?

Choosing a Targeting Approach

  1. The trigger knows nothing about distance — it fires when two shapes overlap. What does the collider do for you that a Vector3.Distance(a, b) call in Update() would make you do by hand, every frame?
  2. inRange is set true on the way in and false on the way out. Name a moment when the player could be inside the circle and your field would still say otherwise.
  3. You have two turrets in this scene and one player. Each turret keeps its own target. What would go wrong if that field were static?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break "the turret notices you" into a shape, a remembered answer, two callbacks and a reference
  • Say why the radius is a collider on a child rather than a number in the script
  • Explain why a trigger needs a Rigidbody2D on one of the two objects to fire at all
  • Name one thing the trigger model cannot tell you, and what you would have to add to know it
  • Say what target is for, and who will read it in 3.2
  • Commit and push
